baslik: A Silent Alarm Blacked Out 55 Million People

sahneler.metin: A silent alarm let a blackout spread across North America.
The outage cascaded until about fifty five million people lost power.
It began in Ohio, in a utility's control room.
A software bug stalled the alarm system there.
Operators never learned that lines were failing.
Overloaded power lines had sagged into overgrown trees.
Each failure pushed more load onto the next line.
Afterwards, grid reliability standards became mandatory.

aciklama:
2003 blackout cut power to an estimated 55 million people. The cause: power lines sagging into trees while a frozen alarm system hid the failures from operators, so the outage cascaded.

kanitlar.iddia: The outage affected an estimated 55 million people.
kanitlar.alinti: The outage, which was much more widespread than the Northeast blackout of 1965, affected an estimated 55 million people, including 10 million people in southern and central Ontario and 45 million people in eight U.S. states.

kanitlar.iddia: The blackout's primary cause was a software bug in the alarm system at the control room of FirstEnergy in Ohio.
kanitlar.alinti: The blackout was due to a software bug in the alarm system at the control room of FirstEnergy, which rendered operators unaware of the need to redistribute load after overloaded transmission lines dropped in voltage.

kanitlar.iddia: Power lines that were overloaded sagged into trees that had not been trimmed.
kanitlar.alinti: The report states that a generating plant in Eastlake, Ohio, a suburb northeast of Cleveland, went offline amid high electrical demand, putting a strain on high-voltage power lines (located in Walton Hills, Ohio, a southeast suburb of Cleveland) which later went out of service when they came in contact with "overgrown trees".

kanitlar.iddia: The blackout led to mandatory reliability standards for the grid.
kanitlar.alinti: On November 19, 2003, Abraham said his department would not seek to punish FirstEnergy Corp for its role in the blackout because current U.S. law does not require electric reliability standards.
